investment_summary:
S&P Global's 2025 results show durable momentum: revenue rose 8% to $15,336 million and diluted EPS rose 19% to $14.66, although about 8 points of operating profit growth came from the one-time OSTTRA gain [1]. Indices (69% operating margin) and Ratings (64%) carry the group, with ETF assets up 25% [1].

Valuation is demanding. At $455.17 the shares trade on 25.4x forward earnings [2][3]. The reverse DCF implies 11.9% annual revenue growth over ten years, close to the 11.1% three-year historical CAGR, yet consensus projects -4.0% revenue for FY2026 and +6.7% for FY2027 [2][3]. At a 10% WACC the implied return is 6.6%, so the price requires growth to return to historical rates and hold there. Consensus data is dated after the 10-K.

The main risks are transaction-driven revenue, regulatory exposure and payouts above free cash flow: $6.2 billion of shareholder returns against $5.1 billion of free cash flow, and net debt of $11.8 billion [1][2].
key_takeaways: Indices and ETF-linked fees should keep compounding, since ETF assets rose 25% to $5.48 trillion and supported a 69% segment margin [1].
Buybacks outrunning free cash flow will keep raising leverage, as $6.2 billion of payouts exceeded $5.1 billion of FCF [1][2].
The stock at 25.4x forward earnings needs growth near the 11.9% historical pace, while consensus shows only 6.7% growth in FY2027 [2][3].
Regulatory and cyber exposure in Ratings, Indices and Energy threatens the multiple, given direct supervision and GDPR fines up to 4% of revenue [1].
business_overview:
S&P Global Inc., incorporated in 1925, provides benchmarks, data, analytics and workflow solutions to the capital, energy and commodity, and automotive markets through five businesses: Market Intelligence, Ratings, Energy, Mobility and Indices [1]. Revenue rose 8% to $15,336 million in 2025 from $14,208 million, and subscription revenue was 51% of the total [1]. Operating margin widened to 42% from 39%, and diluted EPS rose 19% to $14.66 [1][2]. Part of that expansion is non-recurring: a $270 million pre-tax gain on the October 2025 sale of the OSTTRA joint venture contributed about 8 points of the 16% operating profit growth [1].

The highest-margin businesses are Indices, with a 69% operating margin, and Ratings, with 64% [1]. Indices asset-linked fees rose 15% to $1,206 million as ending ETF assets grew 25% to $5.480 trillion, while Ratings billed issuance rose 11%, with high-yield issuance up 17% [1]. Ratings generated the largest operating profit at $3,013 million, up 11%, and Market Intelligence, the largest segment by revenue at $4,916 million, earned a 20% margin [1]. These two franchises matter most because their revenue tracks asset levels and debt issuance rather than headcount.

Portfolio activity was heavy. The company acquired With Intelligence for $1.8 billion, along with ORBCOMM's AIS business, ARC Research and McKinsey PriceMetrix. It sold EDM and thinkFolio in January 2026 and plans to spin off Mobility in mid-2026 [1]. It returned $5.0 billion through buybacks in 2025 and pays a quarterly dividend of $0.97 [1]. At the $455.17 share price used in consensus data, the forward P/E is 25.4x [2][3].
market_position:
S&P Global's end markets are global but weighted to the United States. The US generated $9,322 million, or 61% of 2025 revenue, Europe $3,531 million, Asia $1,640 million and the rest of the world $843 million [1]. The filing calls the company a "leading" provider in several businesses, including ETF benchmarks, but it gives no market share figures, so the position rests on scale and disclosed asset levels rather than a stated share [1]. Revenue of $15.3 billion is roughly twice Moody's and about 6.6 times FactSet's, which makes S&P Global the largest pure-play in this group [4].

Customer concentration is not disclosed. The filing says Mobility serves all global OEMs, most of the world's leading suppliers and the majority of the top North American dealerships, which points to a blue-chip customer base in automotive, although no percentage is given [1]. Market Intelligence and Energy rely on enterprise subscription contracts, and the filing also cites data suppliers and distribution partners that may cancel on short notice [1]. Ratings and Indices depend on issuers and asset managers, which means their customer base is concentrated in large institutions rather than in a broad retail base [1].

Classification: a scaled incumbent (market leader) in benchmarks and ratings, with high barriers to entry from licensing and regulation, rather than a disruptor. The main pressure comes from competitors deploying AI and from free public data, which the filing says could materially reduce demand. That challenges the premium position of the core franchise more than it threatens the existing revenue base [1]. At $455.17 the shares trade on 25.4x forward earnings, so the market is already pricing the incumbent position [2][3].
operating_results:
S&P Global's 2025 revenue rose 8% to $15,336 million, and operating profit rose 16% to $6,478 million, lifting operating margin to 42% from 39% [1]. Operating-related expenses, the cost-of-revenue line, grew 5% to $4,563 million, which lifted gross margin to 70.2% from 69.3% [1]. Selling and general expenses grew faster, up 7% to $3,417 million, and the tax rate rose to 22.6% from 21.5% [1]. Net income attributable to S&P Global rose 16% to $4,471 million, and diluted EPS rose 19% to $14.66, helped by a 2.2% lower share count [1][2].

The headline growth overstates the underlying trend. The OSTTRA disposal gain of about $270 million pre-tax contributed roughly 8 points of the 16% operating profit growth [1]. The MD&A puts underlying operating profit growth at about 11% [1]. By segment, Market Intelligence revenue was $4,916 million (up 6%), Ratings $4,724 million (up 8%), Energy $2,299 million (up 7%), Mobility $1,747 million (up 9%) and Indices $1,850 million (up 14%) [1]. Indices and Ratings deliver the strongest growth and margins [1].

Costs also carried one-time items. Severance was $157 million in 2025, including $56 million in Market Intelligence, and Ratings legal costs of $42 million reduced its growth by about 1 point [1]. Mobility's 21% operating profit gain was flattered by a leadership-transition benefit and a legal recovery; excluding one-time items it rose 11% [1]. Consensus expects FY2026 EPS of $17.94 and FY2027 EPS of $20.15 [3]. However, consensus FY2026 revenue of $14,717 million would imply a 4% decline from 2025, which conflicts with the 8% growth reported in the filing and should be verified before relying on it [2][3].
risk_assessment:
The filing ranks cyber and information security as the first risk. S&P Global holds material non-public information on sovereign and corporate issuers, which makes it a target for state-sponsored actors, and AI-assisted attacks are growing in sophistication [1]. The filing says no cyber incident has had a material adverse effect to date, but it also cannot guarantee its defences, identifies visibility gaps in fragmented security tooling, and warns that some losses may be uninsured [1]. It gives no dollar figure for cyber losses or security spend [1].

Regulatory and legal exposure is the second risk and is concentrated in Ratings, Indices and Energy, which operate under credit rating agency rules, EU and UK benchmark regulation and IOSCO principles [1]. Quantified thresholds include GDPR fines of up to the greater of EUR 20 million or 4% of global revenue, and DPPA liquidated damages of $2,500 per individual [1]. The company says it cannot reasonably estimate most litigation outcomes and may not have adequate insurance or reserves, and that compliance costs may not be passed through to customers [1]. On the financial-quality side, the Beneish M-Score of -2.44 gives no statistical warning sign on earnings quality, and the Altman Z-Score of 4.28 is in the safe zone [2].

The third risk is cyclicality and funding. Transaction and asset-linked revenue, such as issuance-based Ratings fees and ETF-linked Indices fees, is directly exposed to interest rates, credit spreads and market volatility [1]. Funding is the sharpest near-term pressure: 2025 buybacks of $5.0 billion and dividends of $1.17 billion totalled about $6.2 billion, against free cash flow of $5.1 billion [1][2]. Total debt rose to $13.6 billion from $11.9 billion, common equity fell to $31.1 billion from $33.2 billion, current assets of $6.3 billion cover only part of current liabilities of $7.6 billion, and tangible book value is negative $21.6 billion [1]. Consensus latest-quarter data, dated after the 10-K (30 September 2026), show total debt of $13.5 billion, net cash of -$11.0 billion and a current ratio of 0.7 [2].
competitors_analysis:
Peers were chosen by business model first and size second. Moody's (MCO) is the closest, because its Ratings business competes directly with S&P Global Ratings. MSCI competes in index and analytics data, and FactSet (FDS) sells subscription data and analytics to the same financial professionals [4]. Exchanges such as CME and ICE were excluded because their revenue depends on trading volumes, and Verisk because it serves insurers [4].

S&P Global is the largest of the four by revenue, about twice Moody's $7,718 million, 4.9 times MSCI's $3,134 million and 6.6 times FactSet's $2,322 million [4]. Its 2025 revenue growth of 7.9% trailed Moody's 8.9% and MSCI's 9.7%, but was ahead of FactSet's 5.4% [4]. Gross margin of 70.2% sits below Moody's 74.4% and MSCI's 82.4%, and above FactSet's 52.7% [4]. Free cash flow conversion of 1.22 is above Moody's 1.05, MSCI's 1.21 and FactSet's 1.03, which supports the cash-generation case [4].

The returns gap is the main weakness. ROIC of 11.4% is the lowest in the group, against Moody's 24.3%, MSCI's 38.7% and FactSet's 18.1%, and the gap to Moody's has widened to 12.9 points [4]. EBITDA margin of 50.2% matches Moody's 50.4% and trails MSCI's 61.3% [4]. At 20.7 times EV/EBITDA, S&P Global trades below Moody's 24.6 and MSCI's 25.0, and above FactSet's 15.8, a discount that its lower returns help explain [4]. Consensus data, dated after the 10-K, put forward P/E at 25.4x and forward EV/Sales at 10.1x [3].

investment_theses.thesis: Indices asset-linked fees keep growing at mid-teens rates as ETF assets compound, so Indices remains the main earnings driver.
investment_theses.evidence: Asset-linked fees rose 15% to $1,206 million and ending ETF AUM rose 25% to $5.480 trillion; Indices operating margin was 69% [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Indices asset-linked fee growth of at least 10% reported in the FY2026 10-K (filed about February 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Asset-linked fee growth below 5% in FY2026, or ending ETF AUM falling at year end.

investment_theses.thesis: Shareholder payouts above free cash flow are not sustainable without disposal proceeds, so leverage keeps rising.
investment_theses.evidence: 2025 buybacks of $5.0 billion and dividends of $1.17 billion totalled about $6.2 billion against FCF of $5.1 billion; total debt rose to $13.6 billion from $11.9 billion [1][2].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 buybacks plus dividends at or below free cash flow, and total debt growth below 10%, in the FY2026 10-K (about February 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Total debt above $15 billion in FY2026, or payouts above FCF again without material disposal proceeds.

investment_theses.thesis: The current valuation requires revenue growth to return to historical rates, which consensus does not yet forecast.
investment_theses.evidence: Forward P/E is 25.4x at $455.17; the reverse DCF implies 11.9% growth against an 11.1% three-year CAGR, while consensus shows +6.7% for FY2027 and an implied IRR of 6.6% against a 10% WACC [2][3]. Consensus data is dated after the 10-K.
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 consensus EPS at or above $17.94 with more analysts raising than cutting estimates over the next 30 days, confirmed at the FY2026 results (about February 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2027 consensus EPS cut below the $19.60 low end of the current range, or FY2026 reported revenue declining year on year.

investment_theses.thesis: Regulatory and legal costs will not erode the 42% operating margin, so the margin story holds despite supervision in Ratings, Indices and Energy.
investment_theses.evidence: Consolidated operating margin reached 42%, but it includes a $270 million one-time gain; Ratings legal costs of $42 million and severance of $157 million were absorbed; GDPR fines can reach 4% of global revenue [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Operating margin excluding disposal gains of at least 40% in the FY2026 10-K (about February 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Operating margin excluding disposal gains below 38%, or a regulatory fine materially larger than the sanctions previously disclosed.
